content.title: Subject-Verb Agreement: Intervening Phrases and the Proximity Rule
content.overview: Subject-verb agreement requires that a verb matches its subject in number. On the ACT, this is complicated by words that come between the subject and verb, or by compound subjects joined by 'or' or 'nor'.
learning_objectives: Identify the true subject of a sentence by ignoring intervening prepositional phrases and clauses.
Apply the proximity rule to subjects joined by 'or' or 'nor'.
Select the correct singular or plural verb form based on the identified subject.

sections.title: The Core Rule of Agreement
sections.content: A verb must agree in number with its subject. A singular subject requires a singular verb (usually ending in -s in the present tense, like 'runs'), while a plural subject requires a plural verb (like 'run'). The ACT often places nouns between the subject and the verb to distract you. You must ignore these 'intervening' words—such as prepositional phrases starting with 'of', 'in', or 'with'—to find the true subject.

sections.title: The Proximity Rule (Or/Nor)
sections.content: When subjects are joined by the conjunctions 'or' or 'nor' (often as part of 'either...or' or 'neither...nor'), the verb does not automatically become plural. Instead, the verb must agree with the subject closest to it. This is known as the proximity rule or the nearest-subject rule.

sections.title: Identifying Intervening Phrases
sections.content: Intervening phrases often begin with prepositions (e.g., 'The box of chocolates [is/are] empty') or relative pronouns (e.g., 'The player who scored the goals [is/are] tired'). To find the subject, mentally cross out the phrase between the subject and the verb. In the first example, 'of chocolates' is a prepositional phrase; the subject is 'box' (singular), so the verb must be 'is'.

worked_examples.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The collection of rare stamps (was / were) sold at the auction.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the verb: 'was/were'. 2. Identify the subject: 'collection'. 3. Identify the intervening phrase: 'of rare stamps'. 4. Ignore the plural 'stamps' because it is the object of a preposition. 5. Match the singular 'collection' with the singular verb 'was'. Correct: 'The collection... was sold.'

worked_examples.question: Choose the correct verb: 'Neither the coaches nor the players (has / have) arrived yet.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Recognize the 'neither...nor' construction. 2. Identify the two subjects: 'coaches' (plural) and 'players' (plural). 3. Identify the subject closest to the verb: 'players'. 4. Since 'players' is plural, the verb must be plural. Correct: 'Neither the coaches nor the players have arrived yet.'

common_mistakes: Matching the verb to the noun immediately preceding it rather than the true subject.
Assuming that 'neither...nor' always takes a plural verb because two things are mentioned.
Treating prepositional phrases (like 'along with' or 'as well as') as if they create a compound plural subject.
exam_tips: Physically cross out prepositional phrases on your test booklet to see the subject and verb side-by-side.
If you are unsure, simplify the sentence: replace the subject with 'He' or 'They' to see which verb sounds correct.
Watch for 'or' and 'nor'; they are the only triggers for the proximity rule.
content.recap: To ensure subject-verb agreement, identify the true subject by ignoring intervening phrases. For subjects joined by 'or' or 'nor', make the verb agree with the noun closest to it.

knowledge_claims.content: A verb must agree in number (singular or plural) with its subject, regardless of other nouns in the sentence.
To find the true subject, ignore intervening prepositional phrases or clauses located between the subject and the verb.
When subjects are joined by 'or' or 'nor', the verb must agree with the subject closest to the verb.
In the present tense, singular verbs often end in 's' (e.g., 'he walks'), while plural verbs do not (e.g., 'they walk').
It is a mistake to make a verb agree with the object of a prepositional phrase instead of the subject.
In the construction 'Neither A nor B', if B is singular, the verb must be singular.
In the construction 'Either A or B', if B is plural, the verb must be plural.
A reliable check for agreement is to read the subject and the chosen verb together while omitting any intervening words.
An intervening phrase is a group of words, such as a prepositional phrase or relative clause, that separates the subject from its verb.
Phrases like 'as well as', 'along with', and 'in addition to' do not create compound subjects; the verb still agrees only with the initial subject.
The proximity rule is specifically triggered by the conjunctions 'or' and 'nor'.
Unlike 'and', which usually creates a plural subject, 'or' and 'nor' require checking the number of the nearest noun.

ENGLISH PASSAGE 1: The Clock Above Alder Street
[1] After three months of fundraising [[a neighborhood restoration crew began]] to repair the brass clock above Alder Street Market. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a market hall built in 1911, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] wear marks showed that an earlier repairer had reversed two nearly identical wheels. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because replacement parts would have erased those clues. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the crew cleaned and reused the original wheels. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the clock kept accurate time through a week of rain. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.]]

For the underlined verb in [2], which choice is most grammatically acceptable?
F) were
G) was
H) have been
J) being
items.explanation: The head of the subject is the singular noun 'series,' so the singular verb 'was' is required.

ENGLISH PASSAGE 2: Counting After Dark
[1] After several cloudy evenings [[a coastal ecology class began]] to count juvenile crabs in tide pools after sunset. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a protected inlet beside the school, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] the smallest crabs appeared most often under flat stones near eelgrass. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because bright white light changed the animals’ movement. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the class switched to dim red lamps and repeated the first survey. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the second set of counts was more consistent. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the revised method gave park staff a dependable baseline for future surveys.]]

For the underlined verb in [2], which choice is most grammatically acceptable?
F) were
G) have been
H) being
J) was
items.explanation: The head of the subject is the singular noun 'series,' so the singular verb 'was' is required.

videoLesson.title: Verify Nearest-Subject Verb Agreement
videoLesson.description: Recognize which noun is the true subject despite intervening phrases or clauses. Apply the proximity rule: make the verb agree with the subject closest to it.
